In the mountain where the great dragons lived, everything was fire and thunder. They roared so loud the clouds ran away. They breathed flames so high the eagles had to take detours.

All except the smallest dragon, who could only manage a flame about the size of a birthday candle.

The other dragons were kind about it, in the way that very large things are kind to very small things — gently, and from a great distance.

One cold night, a lost sparrow flew into the mountain cave, shivering and too tired to fly another wing-beat. The great dragons tried to help, but their flames were so enormous the poor bird was nearly blown away.

The smallest dragon crept forward. She breathed her tiny flame — no bigger than a matchstick — and held it steady. The sparrow hopped close, fluffed its feathers, and let out a contented chirp.

They sat together all night, the smallest dragon and the smallest bird, sharing the smallest fire in the mountain. And it was, by any measure, exactly enough.

The owl had read every book in the forest. This was not as impressive as it sounds, because there was only one book, and it was written by a beetle who had very strong opinions about bark.

Still, the owl considered herself well-read, and she took her job as the forest librarian very seriously.

Every night she would perch on the highest branch and tell stories to whoever would listen. The trouble was, she only knew the one story — the beetle's book — and it wasn't very exciting.

"Chapter Forty-Seven," she would begin. "In which I discover a particularly satisfying piece of elm bark." The audience would shuffle. Leaves would be examined. Yawns would spread like ripples.

Then one evening, a small rabbit asked, "What if you just... made something up?"

The owl blinked her enormous eyes. Made something up? Was that allowed? She opened her beak, and out came a story about a castle made of moonlight, and a key made of song, and a door that only opened when you laughed.

The forest leaned in. Even the wind stopped to listen. And the owl, for the first time in her life, forgot all about bark.

Deep in the oldest part of the forest, where the trees grew so tall their tops disappeared into clouds, there lived a bear with fur the colour of autumn leaves.

She was not the biggest bear, nor the strongest. But she was the most patient. Every evening she would sit at the edge of the great clearing and watch the sky turn from gold to violet to deep, deep blue.

The smaller animals would come to sit beside her — rabbits, hedgehogs, even the shy little mice — because they knew that nothing bad could happen when the bear was watching.

"What are you looking for?" a tiny mouse once asked her.

The bear smiled. "I'm not looking for anything," she said. "I'm making sure everything is still here."

And so each night she counted the stars, one by one, until she was certain that not a single one had gone missing. Only then would she close her eyes and sleep, knowing the forest was safe for another night.

There was a lake so still that the sky forgot where it ended and the water began.

Birds would fly down toward their own reflections, confused and delighted. Fish would leap up toward the clouds, certain they could touch them.

At the centre of the lake sat a small island, no bigger than a blanket, where a single willow tree grew. Beneath that tree lived a frog who collected dreams.

Every night, when children fell asleep near the lake, their dreams would drift down like dandelion seeds and land softly on the water. The frog would gather them up and plant them in the muddy shore.

By morning, the dreams had grown into small glowing flowers that lasted exactly one day. If you were lucky enough to find one, you could hold it to your ear and hear the dream it came from — a song, a laugh, an adventure not yet taken.

The frog never kept a single dream for himself. "Dreams are meant to be given away," he'd say to no one in particular, and go back to waiting for the night.

The fox woke to find the sky empty. No moon. Not even a sliver.

"It must have fallen," she said, and set off through the midnight forest to find it.

She checked the bottom of the old well. She checked inside the hollow oak. She even checked under Mrs. Badger's porch, which took some courage because Mrs. Badger did not appreciate visitors.

At last she came to the river, and there it was — the moon, sitting in the water, round and bright as a silver coin.

The fox reached in to grab it, but her paw went right through. She tried again. And again. Each time the moon broke into a hundred shimmering pieces, then slowly put itself back together.

She sat back on her haunches, thinking. Then she looked up — and there was the moon, right where it had always been, hanging in the sky above the trees.

"Oh," said the fox. She looked back at the river. The moon was there too. She looked up again. Two moons. "Well," she said, "that's twice as nice." And she trotted home, quite pleased with the world.

Everyone knew that rabbits were good at hopping. But this particular rabbit was good at hopping between places that weren't quite there.

One hop and she'd be in a meadow made entirely of music, where the grass played different notes when the wind blew through it. Another hop and she'd find herself in a library where the books read themselves aloud in sleepy, rumbling voices.

She tried to tell the other rabbits about these places, but they were mostly interested in clover.

"There's a whole world made of rain," she'd say. "Every drop is a tiny bell."

"That's nice," they'd reply. "Have you tried the clover by the south fence? It's exceptional this year."

So the rabbit kept her worlds to herself, visiting them one by one each night after the others had gone to sleep. She'd hop through doorways only she could see, into places only she could find, and return each morning with grass stains on her knees and stars caught in her fur.

Once, long before anyone can remember, the sun was shy.

It would peek over the horizon each morning, see the whole world looking up at it, and duck back down again, blushing orange and pink.

The flowers drooped. The rivers slowed. The children forgot what warmth felt like.

Then one morning, a very small girl walked to the top of the tallest hill. She didn't shout or wave. She simply sat down, closed her eyes, and whispered, "It's okay. You don't have to be bright for everyone. Just be bright for you."

The sun, curious, rose just a little higher to hear her better. Then a little higher still. Before it knew what had happened, it was all the way up in the sky, and the world was warm again.

The girl smiled, eyes still closed, feeling the light on her face. And the sun, for the first time, smiled too.

In the deepest part of the ocean, where the water was so dark it was almost a colour no one had invented yet, there lived a whale who sang.

Her songs were not like other songs. They didn't have beginnings or endings. They were more like questions that didn't need answers, or like the feeling you get when you remember something beautiful that might not have happened.

The other sea creatures would stop what they were doing when she sang. Jellyfish would pause mid-pulse. Crabs would forget which direction they were walking. Even the grumpy old octopus would uncross at least three of his arms.

One day a small fish asked her, "What are your songs about?"

The whale thought for a long time. Whales are good at thinking for a long time.

"They're about the space between things," she said at last. "Between the surface and the deep. Between sleeping and waking. Between one wave and the next."

The small fish didn't entirely understand, but it didn't matter. Understanding wasn't really the point. The point was the listening, and the way the dark water hummed, and the feeling that even in the deepest, darkest place, you were never quite alone.

The oldest tree in the forest had been alive so long it had forgotten its own name. It had watched rivers change their minds about which way to flow. It had seen mountains grow tired and sit down.

Its roots went so deep they touched the dreams of the earth itself — slow, warm dreams about stone and water and the patient work of growing.

Every creature in the forest had carved something into its bark at one time or another. Names, dates, tiny drawings of acorns. The tree didn't mind. It considered these its tattoos, and was rather proud of them.

On autumn evenings, when its leaves turned gold and let go one by one, the tree would tell its stories. Not in words — trees don't use words — but in the way its branches creaked, and the pattern its shadows made, and the particular rustle of each falling leaf.

If you sat very still and listened with your whole self, you could hear them: tales of every bird that had nested in its crown, every storm it had weathered, every spring morning it had watched the world wake up again.

The tree had no ending to its story. It just kept growing, one ring at a time, adding new chapters with every passing year.
